reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it presents Rapido Run as an opportunity to join through an inviter using an ETH startup amount for claimed unlimited or passive earnings. It connects recruiting partners, buying or owning packages, upgrading and filling matrix slots with commissions, redirected payments and projected returns. Although the material is described as educational and the figures as projections, it still shows a financial solicitation and participation flow; completed payments, realized returns and external operation are not established.

opening.argument: The presentation expressly limits its claims and directs viewers toward independent judgment rather than presenting success as certain. Its description says the content is for educational purposes and merely reflects personal opinions, while also advising viewers to research independently and consult a licensed financial adviser. It additionally states that investments involve risk and that success, savings, or avoiding loss are not guaranteed. Those are substantive qualifications accompanying the discussion, not an unconditional promise of profit. The earnings figures are separately characterized as a projection tied to an assumed ETH price, further signaling that they are hypothetical rather than established outcomes.

there is no guarantee that you will be successful in making, saving, or investing money; nor is there any guarantee that you won't
it is just a projection and it was calculated when one ETH it's at $250.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The presence of an entry amount and an invitation link does not erase the explicit risk disclosures. The cited language describes how the proposed system is supposed to work, but it does not establish that payments occurred, that returns were guaranteed, or that viewers were deceived. Indeed, the material expressly says the figures are only a projection and warns that losses are possible. A judge should evaluate those qualifications alongside the promotional language, not treat every explanation of a financial program as proof of fraud.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A disclaimer does not neutralize the conduct the presentation actually promotes. The description pairs the warning with “Life time passive income,” “Only 0.03 ETH,” and earning money by building a team. The speaker also explains that viewers need an inviter and should buy slots so commissions are not bypassed. Risk language may qualify the promise, but it does not change the depicted participation structure or the solicitation to fund and recruit into it.

opening.argument: The video's primary activity is an instructional walkthrough of a smart-contract compensation plan. The presenter says he will use the PDF to explain the plan, then methodically describes the X3, X4, and X8 matrices, slot placement, reinvestment, upgrades, and color coding. The sampled material is a browser screen recording of presentation pages, including slides titled “Ways To Earn,” “REGISTRATION,” “REINVEST,” and “UPGRADE,” which is consistent with demonstrating how the proposed system is structured. Explaining an alleged program's mechanics does not by itself endorse its truth or prove that it operated. The content can reasonably be understood as technology and operational education about a claimed blockchain arrangement.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling the material an explanation does not make it neutral education. The description directs viewers to Telegram groups and calls the system an opportunity for passive income, while the speaker explains how to join through an inviter and how to obtain commissions. The screen recording format shows presentation slides, but it cannot establish that the presenter is testing or criticizing the program. The operational detail is precisely what makes the recruitment and payment flow actionable.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The instructional format is not the issue; the substance is. The walkthrough tells viewers they can earn unlimited ETH, describes recruiting partners beneath them, and says packages are needed to receive commissions. A tutorial can still be promotional when it explains the steps and incentives for participation. The slides therefore support an actionable recruitment pitch, not merely detached technology education.

opening.argument: The evidence does not establish the essential real-world outcomes that would distinguish a fraudulent operation from a presentation about a proposed digital service. It shows a claimed blockchain-based arrangement and diagrams of hypothetical slots, but no supplied source confirms a completed payment, an actual participant, a realized return, or a functioning contract. The presenter even describes the earnings figures as a projection. The material explains claimed allocation rules, including that commissions are distributed “in real time,” but that assertion is not independent proof that the system performed as described. A careful classification should not infer an operating scam solely from diagrams, promotional wording, or an entry price.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The absence of a completed transaction is not decisive when the content itself presents the participation mechanism. The supplied material identifies a startup amount, directs joining through an inviter, places recruited partners under participants, and makes commissions depend on packages or slots. Those are not merely generic service features; they describe the proposed flow of money and recruitment. Whether the contract ultimately functioned is separate from whether the video promotes that scheme.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The missing-outcome point cannot convert this into ordinary commerce. The presentation does not describe a conventional product purchased for ordinary use; it describes slot purchases, referral placement, upline payments, reinvestment, and upgrades to avoid missing commissions. The lack of a completed payment may limit what can be proved about operation, but it does not remove the recruitment-commission mechanism expressly presented to viewers.
